caveats: Finite optimization is over all real weights in the box, normalized by u=beta times w in supporting lemmas. It includes tied outcomes and equal probability bounds; the corrected lower rule and disjoint class tails are essential.

Convergence uses a finite sampling design replicated independently with the same law. Units within a replicate may be dependent, and the pooled estimators are extrema over actual membership indicators; initial empty samples are totalized, with eventual nonemptiness proved.

Sharpness conditional only on limiting shares permits an unknown positive absolute scale and unrestricted finite population size. Actual class proportions must have rational coordinates, so continuous optimizer attainment need not be finite-population attainment.

Retaining absolute class totals or fixing the population size adds integer restrictions; the continuous weight-box interval remains an outer bound and need not be sharp for that richer information set.
The application's ratio condition is a product tradeoff, not a separate lower bound on each ratio. The selected product theorem establishes the algebraic identity, not the full empirical application.

Table arithmetic uses the uniquely inferred counts 44/48, 108/160 and 291/579, rather than recovered source data, and exact rational rounding with half-open nearest-tenth intervals; no corrected cell is a rounding tie.

corrections.what: Proposition 1 prints the lower stopping inequality in the wrong direction; replacing it by $\le$ yields first-cut threshold weights attaining the minimum and maximum over $[1/\beta,1/\alpha]^n$ for a nonempty sorted real sample and $0<\alpha\le\beta\le1$, and the complete attainable set is the closed interval between them, also for arbitrary positive masses and sorted real outcomes.

Proposition 2 uses the wrong lower stopping inequality and overlapping lower-tail sums; with the corrected $\le$ test and disjoint prefix and tail, the first-cut vectors attain both variational endpoints for strictly ordered outcome classes with positive totals and $0<\alpha\le\beta\le1$.

The application claims that each of two directional selection ratios must exceed three; for interior sampled prevalences $p_E<p_G$ and positive stratum selection probabilities, equal inverse-probability reweighted prevalences instead impose the product identity $(g_1/g_0)(e_0/e_1)=p_G(1-p_E)/(p_E(1-p_G))$.

The text calls Assumption 2 necessary for convergence; under iid replication of any finite sampling design with $0<\alpha\le\pi_i\le\beta\le1$, the actual pooled sample is eventually nonempty almost surely and both optimized endpoints converge almost surely to their population class endpoints without Assumption 2.

Proposition 2's sharpness claim requires an information-set qualification: conditional only on positive limiting sampled-outcome shares, unrestricted population size and at least one compatible population, the variational endpoints are the infimum and supremum of compatible finite-population means, with an endpoint attained exactly when an optimizing population-proportion vector has rational coordinates.

Table 1 uses rounded sample percentages to compute bounds; exact proportions inferred from the reported counts give certified nearest-tenth rounding for all 42 bounds, with six entries one tenth of a percentage point below their printed values.

key_results.what: For a nonempty finite real sample and $0<\alpha\le\beta\le1$, the entire attainable weighted-mean set depends only on $\gamma=\beta/\alpha$, and at $\gamma=1$ it is the singleton ordinary sample mean.
For a sorted nonempty sample and $\gamma\ge1$, every pair of equal outcomes receives equal weights in both the corrected first-cut lower optimizer and the first-cut upper optimizer.

For any nonempty binary sample with ordinary proportion $p$ and $0<\alpha\le\beta\le1$, the entire attainable weighted-mean set is $[p/(\gamma(1-p)+p),\,\gamma p/((1-p)+\gamma p)]$, where $\gamma=\beta/\alpha$, including $p=0$, $p=1$ and $\gamma=1$.

overview.overview: The paper bounds a population mean when selection probabilities are unknown but lie between known positive limits, using extrema of the Hajek ratio over a weight box. The Lean development proves corrected threshold optimizers, binary-outcome formulas and almost-sure convergence of pooled-sample extrema under independent replication. It also formalizes the distinction between continuous weight optimization and finite-population sharpness, repairs the selection-ratio interpretation in the needle-prevalence application and checks its table arithmetic.

text.body: The Lean statements formalize the two-unit example of P025-E001, namely the sample $y=(0,1)$ with $\alpha=1/2$, $\beta=1$ and $\gamma=2$. For $0\leqslant k\leqslant n$, let $F^{\mathrm L}_k=\{\gamma\sum_{i\leqslant k}y_i+\sum_{i>k}y_i\}/\{\gamma k+(n-k)\}$ be the left side of the rule for $k^{\mathrm L}$. The main statement asserts that the printed rule, with $\geqslant$, returns $k^{\mathrm L}=0$, that $F^{\mathrm L}_0=1/2$ and $F^{\mathrm L}_1=1/3$, and that $1/3\leqslant v/(u+v)\leqslant 2/3$ for all $(u,v)\in[1,2]^2$, where $(u,v)=(\beta w_1,\beta w_2)$ are the weights of (3) multiplied by $\beta$. By these assertions, the minimum of (3) is $1/3$, and the printed lower bound $1/2$ exceeds it by $1/6$. A second statement asserts that the set of values of $w'y/(w'1_n)$ over the box $[1/\beta,1/\alpha]^2$ is $[1/3,2/3]$, and that $1/3$ does not lie in $[1/2,2/3]$, the interval of (5) computed with the printed $k^{\mathrm L}$. A third statement describes a design that produces the sample. In a population of two units with outcomes $(0,1)$, the design selects the second unit alone or both units, each with probability $1/2$, and the statement asserts that the inclusion probabilities are $(1/2,1)$ and that both units are sampled with probability $1/2$. Two further statements use the mass-weighted version $F^{\mathrm L}_k=\{\gamma\sum_{i\leqslant k}a_iy_i+\sum_{i>k}a_iy_i\}/\{\gamma\sum_{i\leqslant k}a_i+\sum_{i>k}a_i\}$ with $a_i>0$, so that with $a_j=\Pi_j$ they cover the rule for $k_-$ of Proposition 2. They assert that the printed rule returns $0$ for every sample $y_1\leqslant\cdots\leqslant y_n$ with $n\geqslant 1$, and that, for $\gamma>1$ and outcomes that are not all equal, $F^{\mathrm L}_1<F^{\mathrm L}_0$ and $F^{\mathrm L}_0$ is not the minimum of the ratio over the box.

text.body: The Lean statement formalizes the two-class example of P025-E001. The population has two units with outcomes $(0,1)$ and inclusion probabilities $(1/2,1)$, and $\alpha=1/2$, $\beta=1$ and $\gamma=2$. Each outcome class is a single unit, and $(\Pi_1,\Pi_2)=(1/2,1)$. The statement asserts that both probabilities lie in $[\alpha,\beta]$, that the population mean is $1/2$, and that the printed rule, with $\geqslant$, returns $k_-=0$. It asserts that the ratio in (7) equals $2/3$ at the vector with cut point $0$ and $1/2$ at the vector with cut point $1$, and that $1/2\leqslant v/(u/2+v)\leqslant 4/5$ for all $(u,v)\in[1,2]^2$, where $(u,v)=(\beta W_1,\beta W_2)$. By these assertions, the minimum of (7) is $1/2$, which is smaller than the value $2/3$ at the printed $W_-$. The statement also records that the formula for $\mu_+$ equals $4/5$ at the cut point $1$ and that Assumption 2 holds in the example. The design selects the second unit alone or both units, each with probability $1/2$, and it is the subject of a separate statement shared with the counterexample to Proposition 1. The printed display for $\mu_-$, whose lower limits are corrected in P025-E002, is not evaluated here.

text.body: The Lean statement asserts Proposition 1 with $\leqslant$ in the rule for $k^{\mathrm L}$, as corrected in P025-E001, together with equation (5). Let $n\geqslant 1$, let $y_1\leqslant\cdots\leqslant y_n$ be real, let $0<\alpha\leqslant\beta\leqslant 1$ and $\gamma=\beta/\alpha$, and let $A$ be the set of values of $w'y/(w'1_n)$ as $w$ ranges over $[1/\beta,1/\alpha]^n$. Let $F^{\mathrm L}_k$ and $F^{\mathrm H}_k$ be the left sides of the rules for $k^{\mathrm L}$ and $k^{\mathrm H}$. The statement asserts that there exist a smallest $k^{\mathrm L}\in\{0,\ldots,n-1\}$ such that $F^{\mathrm L}_k\leqslant y_{k+1}$ and a smallest $k^{\mathrm H}\in\{0,\ldots,n-1\}$ such that $F^{\mathrm H}_k\leqslant y_{k+1}$. It asserts that $F^{\mathrm L}_{k^{\mathrm L}}$ is the minimum of $A$, that $F^{\mathrm H}_{k^{\mathrm H}}$ is its maximum, and that $A=[F^{\mathrm L}_{k^{\mathrm L}},F^{\mathrm H}_{k^{\mathrm H}}]$. Tied outcomes, $n=1$ and $\gamma=1$ are included. The set on the left side of (5) is represented by $A$, that is, by the weight vectors $w_i=1/\pi_i$ in the box, and no sampling design enters. The search range $0\leqslant k<n$, which is implicit in the printed $y_{k+1}$, is written out. A companion statement asserts the same conclusions with positive masses $a_i$ in place of unit masses, and adds that $w^{\mathrm L}$ and $w^{\mathrm H}$ lie in the box and that the ratio at these vectors equals $F^{\mathrm L}_{k^{\mathrm L}}$ and $F^{\mathrm H}_{k^{\mathrm H}}$. One supporting statement takes any two feasible normalized vectors $u,v$ and any $z$ between their ratios, and returns $t\in[0,1]$ such that $(1-t)u+tv$ is feasible and has ratio $z$. It allows arbitrary positive masses; common rescaling transfers the statement from $[1,\gamma]^n$ to $[1/\beta,1/\alpha]^n$. Endpoint equality is included. The other supporting statements give the steps, among them the identity for $F_{k+1}-F_k$, the existence of the cut points, and the comparison of the ratio at an arbitrary vector of the box with the ratio at each of the two optimal vectors.

text.body: The Lean statement asserts the part of Proposition 2 that follows the word “Specifically”. It has $\leqslant$ in the rule for $k_-$, as corrected in P025-E001, and the second sums of the formula for $\mu_-$ start at $j=k_-+1$, as corrected in P025-E002. Let $J=|Y|\geqslant 1$, $y_{(1)}<\cdots<y_{(J)}$, $\Pi_j>0$, $0<\alpha\leqslant\beta\leqslant 1$ and $\gamma=\beta/\alpha$, and let $\mu_-$ and $\mu_+$ be the infimum and the supremum of the ratio in (6) and (7) over the box $[1/\beta,1/\alpha]^J$. The statement asserts that there exist smallest indices $k_-$ and $k_+$ in $\{0,\ldots,J-1\}$ that satisfy the two rules. It asserts that the two displayed formulas, evaluated at these cut points, are the minimum and the maximum of the ratio over the box, and that they equal $\mu_-$ and $\mu_+$. The weighted-bounds statement described in P025-T3, which also applies to Proposition 1, asserts in addition that $W_-$ and $W_+$ lie in the box and that the ratio at these vectors equals the two formulas. The totals $\Pi_j$ are arbitrary positive numbers and are not required to be sums of inclusion probabilities, so that the statement is broader than the printed one in this respect. It makes no claim that the optimal vectors are unique. The first sentence of the proposition, on sharpness for $\mu$, is not part of this statement and has its own Lean statement.

text.body: The Lean statements formalize designs A and B of P025-E003, in which the shooting gallery and needle exchange populations have equal prevalence and one of the two selection ratios is below three. Let $r_G$ be the ratio of the selection probability of an infected gallery needle to that of an uninfected one, and let $r_E$ be the reverse ratio for exchange needles. For a sample with infected fraction $p$ and selection probabilities $\pi_1$ and $\pi_0$ for infected and uninfected needles, the Hajek estimate is $(p/\pi_1)/\{p/\pi_1+(1-p)/\pi_0\}$. The main statement asserts that, in design A, both prevalences are $3/4$, the samples are $44$ of $48$ and $291$ of $579$, the probabilities $(11/12,1/4)$ and $(97/288,1)$ lie in $[1/4,1]$, both Hajek estimates equal $3/4$, and $r_G=11/3>3$ while $r_E=288/97<3$. It asserts that, in design B, both prevalences and both estimates are $4/5$, the probabilities $(11/12,1/3)$ and $(291/1156,288/289)$ again lie in $[1/4,1]$, and $r_G=11/4<3$ while $r_E=384/97>3$. It also asserts that $3/4$ and $4/5$ lie between the lower bound for the gallery sample and the upper bound for the exchange sample at $\gamma=4$. A second statement takes the proportions $0.917$ and $0.503$ as exact and gives the two further choices of probabilities in the finding, with $r_E=1491/503<3$ at prevalence $3/4$ and $r_G=917/332<3$ at prevalence $4/5$. In both designs a fixed number $s$ of needles is drawn uniformly from the $N$ infected needles of each population, and likewise from the uninfected ones. Three statements assert that such a draw is a probability distribution, that each needle is selected with probability $s/N$, and that for the seven pairs $(N,s)$ of the two designs these probabilities are the ones used above. The four draws of a design are treated one at a time, and their combination into one design with independent draws is not formalized. The Hajek estimate is evaluated by the formula above at the sample fraction, which does not vary from draw to draw.

text.body: The Lean statements give the mathematical content of the sentences that replace the printed one in P025-E003. Let $L(p,\gamma)=p/\{\gamma(1-p)+p\}$ and $H(p,\gamma)=\gamma p/\{(1-p)+\gamma p\}$ be the endpoints of the closed form for dichotomous outcomes on p. 237, and let $K=p_G(1-p_E)/\{(1-p_G)p_E\}$. The main statement asserts that, for $0<p_E<p_G<1$ and $\gamma\geqslant 1$, the intervals $[L(p_G,\gamma),H(p_G,\gamma)]$ and $[L(p_E,\gamma),H(p_E,\gamma)]$ intersect if and only if $L(p_G,\gamma)\leqslant H(p_E,\gamma)$, and that this holds if and only if $\gamma^2\geqslant K$. A second statement asserts that $K=455749/41749$ and $3.30^2<K<3.31^2$ for the printed proportions $0.917$ and $0.503$, that $K=1056/97$ and $3.29^2<K<3.30^2$ for the proportions $44/48$ and $291/579$, and that $9<K<16$ in both cases. Two statements concern the ratios $r_G=\pi_{G,1}/\pi_{G,0}$ and $r_E=\pi_{E,0}/\pi_{E,1}$ of positive selection probabilities that are constant within infection status. They assert that the two Hajek estimates are equal if and only if $r_Gr_E=K$, and that $K\leqslant\gamma^2$ whenever $r_Gr_E=K$, $r_G\leqslant\gamma$ and $r_E\leqslant\gamma$. The second statement also records that the pairs $(11/3,288/97)$ and $(11/4,384/97)$ have product $1056/97$, with one ratio below three in each. The words “at least about $3{\cdot}30$” are represented by the exact condition $\gamma^2\geqslant K$ and the two brackets for $K$, and the intervals are those of the closed form, which is not derived here from (2) and (3). Four supporting statements assert that the denominators are positive, that $L\leqslant H$, that $L$ is nondecreasing in $p$, and that the Hajek estimate equals its cross-multiplied form.

text.body: The main Lean statement asserts the negation of the universal optimizer and interval assertion in Proposition 1 and equation (5), with the rule for $k^{\mathrm L}$ as printed. Let $n\geqslant 1$, let $y_1\leqslant\cdots\leqslant y_n$ be real, let $0<\alpha\leqslant\beta\leqslant 1$ and $\gamma=\beta/\alpha$, and let $A$ be the set of values of $w'y/(w'1_n)$ as $w$ ranges over $[1/\beta,1/\alpha]^n$. Let $F^{\mathrm L}_k$ and $F^{\mathrm H}_k$ be the left sides of the rules for $k^{\mathrm L}$ and $k^{\mathrm H}$. The assertion being negated requires that there exist a smallest $k^{\mathrm L}\in\{0,\ldots,n-1\}$ such that $F^{\mathrm L}_k\geqslant y_{k+1}$ and a smallest $k^{\mathrm H}\in\{0,\ldots,n-1\}$ such that $F^{\mathrm H}_k\leqslant y_{k+1}$. It requires that $F^{\mathrm L}_{k^{\mathrm L}}$ and $F^{\mathrm H}_{k^{\mathrm H}}$ are the minimum and the maximum of $A$, and that $A$ is the interval between them. The sign $\geqslant$ in the first rule is the only difference between this printed optimizer and interval assertion and the assertion for the corrected proposition. The search range $0\leqslant k<n$ is written out, since $y_{k+1}$ is defined only there. The left side of (5) is printed with $\pi_N$, and the statement reads it as the set of values of $\hat\mu$ over the weights $w_i=1/\pi_i$ of the $n$ sampled units. A second statement isolates the upper half, namely the rule for $k^{\mathrm H}$, the vector $w^{\mathrm H}$ and equation (4), which the correction in P025-E001 leaves as printed.
text.headline: Proposition 1 and equation (5), as printed
text.location: p. 236 (PDF p. 2); Appendix, pp. 239–240 (PDF pp. 5–6)

text.body: Three Lean statements cover the proposition as printed. In all three, $J=|Y|\geqslant 1$, $y_{(1)}<\cdots<y_{(J)}$, the totals $\Pi_j$ are arbitrary positive numbers, $0<\alpha\leqslant\beta\leqslant 1$, and $\mu_-$ and $\mu_+$ are the infimum and the supremum of the ratio in (6) and (7) over the box. The first statement negates the universal algebraic optimizer and formula assertion, retaining the sign $\geqslant$ in the rule for $k_-$ and the lower limits $j=k_--1$ in the formula for $\mu_-$. The assertion being negated requires that the cut points $k_-$ and $k_+$ of the printed rules exist, and that the ratio at $W_-$ and at $W_+$ is the minimum and the maximum over the box. It requires further that the printed formula for $\mu_-$ has a value at $k_-$, that this value is $\mu_-$, and that the formula for $\mu_+$ equals $\mu_+$. For $k_-=0$ and $k_-=1$ the printed lower limit is not the index of a class, and the formula is treated as having no value there. The second statement negates the universal sharpness assertion obtained from the first sentence of the proposition under the reading in which the absolute totals $\Pi_j$ are retained with fixed $\alpha$ and $\beta$. The assertion being negated requires that, whenever some positive integers $m_j$ satisfy $\alpha m_j\leqslant\Pi_j\leqslant\beta m_j$ for all $j$, $\mu_-$ and $\mu_+$ are the infimum and the supremum of the means $\sum_jm_jy_{(j)}/\sum_jm_j$ over all such $m_j$. The printed sentence does not name the information, and the reading with the limiting shares only has its own Lean statement. The third statement isolates the upper half, namely the rule for $k_+$, the vector $W_+$ and the formula for $\mu_+$. The words “in the limit $h\to\infty$” enter only through the totals $\Pi_j$, and no limit is taken.
text.headline: Proposition 2, as printed
text.location: pp. 237–238 (PDF pp. 3–4); supplementary material, pp. 1–2

text.body: The Lean statements give the content of the correction in P025-E002. Let $J=|Y|$, $0<\alpha\leqslant\beta$ and $\gamma=\beta/\alpha$, and for an integer $0\leqslant k\leqslant J$ let $W^{(k)}$ have its first $k$ entries equal to $1/\alpha$ and the others equal to $1/\beta$. The first statement asserts that the ratio in (7) at $W^{(k)}$ equals $R_k=\frac{\gamma\sum_{j=1}^{k}\Pi_jy_{(j)}+\sum_{j=k+1}^{J}\Pi_jy_{(j)}}{\gamma\sum_{j=1}^{k}\Pi_j+\sum_{j=k+1}^{J}\Pi_j}$ for every such $k$, including $k=0$ and $k=J$. The Lean identity also allows $k>J$, with all classes in the first block and an empty second block. A second statement asserts that, for $y_{(1)}<\cdots<y_{(J)}$ and $\Pi_j>0$, the infimum $\mu_-$ in (7) equals $R_{k_-}$ at the cut point $k_-$ of the corrected rule, which is the corrected display. Three statements describe the printed limits. For $2\leqslant k\leqslant J$, the printed second sums contain the classes $k-1$ and $k$ in addition to the classes $j>k$. With $N_k$ and $D_k$ the numerator and the denominator of $R_k$, the printed expression equals $\{N_k+\Pi_{k-1}y_{(k-1)}+\Pi_ky_{(k)}\}/\{D_k+\Pi_{k-1}+\Pi_k\}$ and differs from $R_k$ by $\{\Pi_{k-1}(y_{(k-1)}-R_k)+\Pi_k(y_{(k)}-R_k)\}/\{D_k+\Pi_{k-1}+\Pi_k\}$. For $k=0$ and $k=1$ the printed expression has no value. A sixth statement asserts the first identity for arbitrary weights on the two blocks of classes. The first statement does not depend on how the cut point is chosen, and the second uses the rule as corrected in P025-E001.

text.location: Proposition 2, p. 237 (PDF p. 3)

text.body: The Lean statements formalize the example of P025-E002. The population has six units with outcomes $(0,0,1,1,2,3)$ and inclusion probabilities $(1/2,1/2,1/2,1/2,1,1)$, and $\alpha=1/2$, $\beta=1$ and $\gamma=2$. The distinct outcomes are $(0,1,2,3)$ and $\Pi=(1,1,1,1)$. The main statement asserts that the corrected rule returns $k_-=2$ and that the ratio in (7) at the vector with this cut point is $7/6$. It asserts that the ratio is at least $7/6$ at every vector of the box, taken in the scaled form $[1,2]^4$. It asserts that the printed formula, with second sums from $j=k_--1$, equals $1$ at $k_-=2$. It also asserts that the printed rule for $k_-$ returns $0$, where the printed formula has no value because the lower limit is not the index of a class. The formula is evaluated at the corrected cut point, so that the example separates the error in the limits of summation from the error in the rule. A second statement describes the design, which selects one of the two units with outcome $0$, one of the two units with outcome $1$ and both remaining units, the four possible draws being equally likely. It asserts the inclusion probabilities above, the totals $\Pi_j=1$, the class sizes $(2,2,1,1)$ and the population mean $7/6$.

text.location: Proposition 2, p. 237 (PDF p. 3)

text.body: The Lean statements give the proof steps as corrected in P025-E004, with the case $\gamma=1$ separated. For the Appendix, let $F_k=\{\sum_{i\leqslant k}a_iy_i+\gamma\sum_{i>k}a_iy_i\}/\{\sum_{i\leqslant k}a_i+\gamma\sum_{i>k}a_i\}$ with positive masses $a_i$, where the Appendix has $a_i=1$. One statement asserts that, for $\gamma=1$ and unit masses, $F_k$ equals the sample mean for every $k$ and the box of scaled weights is the single point $(1,\ldots,1)$. Another statement asserts, for every $\gamma\ge1$, $F_{k+1}-F_k=\frac{(1-\gamma)\,a_{k+1}\,(y_{k+1}-F_k)}{D_{k+1}}\qquad\text{for } 0\leqslant k<n,$ where $D_{k+1}$ is the denominator of $F_{k+1}$, and, under the additional condition $\gamma>1$, equality of the stationary-test and outcome-test index sets: $F_k\geqslant F_{k+1}$ if and only if $F_k\leqslant y_{k+1}$. Thus the two minima on p. 240 agree for $\gamma>1$; they are not identified at $\gamma=1$. A third asserts that $F_k\leqslant y_{k+1}$ implies $F_{k+1}\leqslant y_{k+1}$ for $\gamma\geqslant 1$. For the supplementary material, let $\mu(x,z)=(c_1+xpu+zqv)/(c_2+xp+zq)$ with $c_2\geqslant 0$, $p,q>0$, $u<v$ and $0<a\leqslant b$, where $a=1/\beta$, $b=1/\alpha$, $p=\Pi_k$, $q=\Pi_{k+1}$, $u=y_{(k)}$ and $v=y_{(k+1)}$. The main statement asserts that, if $a<b$, then $\mu(a,a)>\mu(b,a)$ if and only if (B1) holds, $\mu(b,b)>\mu(b,a)$ if and only if (B2) holds, and at least one of the two inequalities holds, and that, if $a=b$, then $\mu(a,a)=\mu(b,a)=\mu(b,b)$. A fifth statement asserts the two identities of the finding, in which each difference carries the factor $a-b$, and the identity for the sum of the left sides of (B1) and (B2), which is negative. The existence of the cut point and the value of (4) at $\gamma=1$ are part of the statement for Proposition 1 as corrected, and the sentence of the correction that (6) and (7) both equal $\mu$ when $\alpha=\beta$ has no statement of its own.
text.headline: Appendix, proof of Proposition 1, and steps (B1) and (B2) of the supplementary material, as corrected
text.location: Appendix, pp. 239–240 (PDF pp. 5–6); supplementary material, p. 2

text.body: The Lean statements formalize the example of P025-E004, in which $n=N=2$, $y=(0,1)$ and $\alpha=\beta=1$, so that $\gamma=1$. With $F_k=(w^{k\prime}y)/(w^{k\prime}1_n)$, the main statement asserts that $F_0=F_1=F_2=1/2$. It asserts that $F_1-F_0\leqslant 0$ holds and that $F_0\leqslant y_1$ fails, which contradicts the implication on p. 239 at $k=0$. It asserts that the smallest $k\in\{0,1\}$ such that $F_k\geqslant F_{k+1}$ is $0$ and that the smallest $k$ such that $F_k\leqslant y_{k+1}$ is $1$, so that the two minima on p. 240 differ. For the supplementary material, it asserts that the left sides of (B1) and (B2) both equal $-1$ when $c_1=c_2=0$ and $\Pi_1=\Pi_2=1$. The weight pairs $(1/\beta,1/\beta)$, $(1/\alpha,1/\beta)$ and $(1/\alpha,1/\alpha)$ coincide in the example, and the failure of the two strict inequalities is expressed by the assertion that the ratio at the weights $(1,1)$ does not exceed itself. In this respect the statement is narrower than the printed steps, since it does not use the function $\mu(\cdot,\cdot)$ of the supplementary material. A second statement asserts that the census, which selects both units with probability one, has inclusion probabilities $(1,1)$. The statements contradict steps of the two proofs and not Proposition 1 or Proposition 2.
text.headline: A counterexample to the Appendix proof of Proposition 1 and to steps (B1) and (B2) of the supplementary material, as printed
text.location: Appendix, pp. 239–240 (PDF pp. 5–6); supplementary material, p. 2

text.body: The main Lean statement asserts the stronger form of Proposition 3 in P025-E005, in which Assumption 2 is not a hypothesis. A sampling design is a probability distribution on finitely many draws, each of which selects a subset of a population of $N\geqslant 1$ units. Every design on a finite population has this form, with any dependence among the indicators within a draw. The inclusion probabilities satisfy $0<\alpha\leqslant\pi_i\leqslant\beta\leqslant 1$, and the units are divided into $J$ nonempty classes with outcomes $y_{(1)}<\cdots<y_{(J)}$. Assumption 1 is represented by the infinite product of the design, under which the successive draws are independent and identically distributed. The estimators $\hat\mu_h^{\mathrm L}$ and $\hat\mu_h^{\mathrm H}$ are the infimum and the supremum of the ratio in (3) and (2) over the box of weights, for the sample pooled over the first $h$ draws, in which a unit counts once for each draw that selects it. The limits $\mu_-$ and $\mu_+$ are the same quantities for (7) and (6) with the totals $\Pi_j$ of the design. The statement asserts that, for almost every sequence of draws, the pooled sample is nonempty for all large $h$, and $\hat\mu_h^{\mathrm L}\to\mu_-$ and $\hat\mu_h^{\mathrm H}\to\mu_+$. Twenty supporting statements give the steps. Among them are the equality of the estimators with the extrema of $f(W,P_h)$ over the box and the bound $\bigl|f(W,p)-f(W,\Pi)\bigr|\leqslant\frac{\gamma R}{S}\sum_j|p_j-\Pi_j|$ of the finding, for $p_j\geqslant 0$, $\sum_jp_j>0$ and $W\in[1/\beta,1/\alpha]^J$, with $R=y_{(J)}-y_{(1)}$ and $S=\sum_j\Pi_j$. Others assert that the count of class $j$ in one draw has mean $\Pi_j$, and that $P_{h,j}\to\Pi_j$ almost surely for every $j$. The reworded sentence before Assumption 2 has no separate statement here. Proposition 3 with both assumptions and with hats has its own Lean statement, in which Assumption 2 has the range $0\leqslant k<|Y|$.
text.headline: Section 3.2, the sentence before Assumption 2, Assumption 2 and Proposition 3, as corrected
text.location: Section 3.2, p. 238 (PDF p. 4); supplementary material, p. 2

text.body: The Lean statements formalize the example of P025-E005. The population has six units with outcomes $(0,0,2,2,3,3)$, each draw selects one unit from each pair of units with equal outcomes, the eight possible draws are equally likely, and $\alpha=1/4$, $\beta=1/2$ and $\gamma=2$. The main statement asserts that every inclusion probability lies in $[1/4,1/2]$, that Assumption 2 fails for the totals of the design, and that $\mu_-=5/4$ and $\mu_+=2$. It asserts that, for every sequence of draws and every $h\geqslant 1$, the bounds computed from the sample pooled over the first $h$ draws are $\hat\mu_h^{\mathrm L}=5/4$ and $\hat\mu_h^{\mathrm H}=2$. It asserts further that both sequences converge to these values on every sequence of draws, which is stronger than the almost sure convergence of Proposition 3. The estimators and the limits are represented as in the statement for Proposition 3 as corrected, as the infimum and the supremum of the ratio over the box of weights. Six further statements give the parts, beginning with the assertions that every $\pi_i$ equals $1/2$, that every $\Pi_j$ equals $1$, and that every draw contains one unit of each class. They assert that the first ratio of Assumption 2 at $k=1$ equals $y_{(2)}=2$, and that the ratio in (6) and (7) has minimum $5/4$ and maximum $2$ over $[2,4]^3$. The same extrema are asserted for a sample with $h$ units at each of the three outcomes, for every $h\geqslant 1$. The statements contradict the claim that the condition is necessary, and they do not contradict Proposition 3, which states that the condition is sufficient.
text.headline: A counterexample to the sentence “A mild technical condition on $k_+$ and $k_-$ is necessary to guarantee convergence”, as printed
text.location: Section 3.2, the sentence before Assumption 2, p. 238 (PDF p. 4)

text.body: The main Lean statement asserts the claim of sharpness as qualified in P025-N002, where only the limiting shares $q_j=\Pi_j/\sum_k\Pi_k$ are retained and the population size is unrestricted. Let $y_{(1)}<\cdots<y_{(J)}$, $q_j>0$ with $\sum_jq_j=1$, $0<\alpha\leqslant\beta\leqslant 1$ and $\gamma=\beta/\alpha$, and let $\mu_-$ and $\mu_+$ be (7) and (6) with $q_j$ in place of $\Pi_j$. A compatible population is represented by its class sizes, which are positive integers $m_j$ such that $\alpha m_j\leqslant Tq_j\leqslant\beta m_j$ for all $j$ and some $T>0$, and its mean is $\sum_jm_jy_{(j)}/\sum_jm_j$. Under the hypothesis that at least one compatible population exists, which is a restriction only for $\gamma=1$, the statement asserts that $\mu_-$ and $\mu_+$ are the infimum and the supremum of the means of the compatible populations. It asserts that the map $W\mapsto(W_jq_j/\sum_kW_kq_k)_j$ sends the box $[1/\beta,1/\alpha]^J$ onto the set $\mathcal C_\gamma(q)$ of the finding, and that $r$ is the vector of class proportions of a compatible population if and only if $r\in\mathcal C_\gamma(q)$ and $r$ has rational coordinates. It asserts that $\mu_-$ is the mean of a compatible population if and only if $\sum_jr_jy_{(j)}=\mu_-$ for some rational $r\in\mathcal C_\gamma(q)$, and likewise for $\mu_+$. A supporting statement asserts that the condition on $m_j$ holds if and only if there exist numbers $\pi_i\in[\alpha,\beta]$, one for each of the $m_j$ units, with sum $Tq_j$, and a sampling design with these inclusion probabilities is not constructed. Further statements assert that $[\mu_-,\mu_+]$ contains the mean of every compatible population, also when the totals $\Pi_j$ are retained, in which case the class sizes are the positive integers in $[\Pi_j/\beta,\Pi_j/\alpha]$. The remaining statements give the steps, such as the density of the rational points when $\gamma>1$. The words “in the limit $h\to\infty$” are represented by taking the shares as given, and no limit is taken.
text.headline: Proposition 2, first sentence, as corrected
text.location: Section 3.2, p. 237 (PDF p. 3); also Section 1, p. 235 (PDF p. 1), and p. 238 (PDF p. 4)

text.body: The Lean statements formalize the two examples of P025-N002 in which more than the limiting shares is retained. A compatible population is represented by its class sizes, which are positive integers $m_j$ such that $\alpha m_j\leqslant\Pi_j\leqslant\beta m_j$, and its mean is $\sum_jm_jy_{(j)}/\sum_jm_j$. In the first example the outcomes are $(0,1)$, $\Pi=(2/3,4/3)$, $\alpha=1/2$ and $\beta=3/4$. The main statement asserts that the set of compatible means is $\{2/3\}$, that $4/7$ is not its infimum and that $3/4$ is not its supremum. Further statements assert that the only compatible class sizes are $(1,2)$, that the ratio in (6) and (7) has minimum $4/7$ and maximum $3/4$ over the box, and that Assumption 2 holds. They assert that the design on three units with outcomes $(0,1,1)$ which selects each pair of units with probability $1/3$ has every $\pi_i$ equal to $2/3$ and the totals above. In the second example $\Pi=(50,100)$, $\alpha=1/10$, $\beta=1/5$, and the class sizes sum to $N=1000$. The statements assert that the compatible class sizes are those with $500\leqslant m_2\leqslant 750$, that the set of compatible means is $\{k/1000:500\leqslant k\leqslant 750\}$ with maximum $3/4$, and that $\mu_+=4/5$ exceeds this maximum by $1/20$. No design is constructed in the second example, where compatibility is the condition on the class sizes. The printed sentence does not name the information, and these statements concern the reading in which the totals are retained with fixed $\alpha$ and $\beta$. They do not contradict the claim for shares only, which has its own Lean statement.
text.headline: A counterexample to the first sentence of Proposition 2, as printed
text.location: Section 3.2, p. 237 (PDF p. 3); supplementary material, p. 2

text.body: The Lean statements recalculate Table 1 as in P025-N003, in exact rational arithmetic. Let $L(p,\gamma)=p/\{\gamma(1-p)+p\}$ and $H(p,\gamma)=\gamma p/\{(1-p)+\gamma p\}$, and say that $x$ rounds to $t/10$ when $t/10-1/20\leqslant x<t/10+1/20$. The 42 cells are entered as data, each with its value of $\gamma$, its bound, the printed entry and the corrected entry. The main statement asserts that, in every cell, $100L$ or $100H$ at the proportion from the counts ($44/48$, $108/160$ or $291/579$) rounds to the corrected entry, and that the same quantity at the rounded proportion ($0.917$, $0.675$ or $0.503$) rounds to the printed entry. It asserts that the printed and the corrected entries differ in exactly six cells, and that the printed entry is $0.1$ higher in each of them. A second statement asserts that $44$, $108$ and $291$ are the only integers $k$ such that $100k/48$, $100k/160$ and $100k/579$ are within $0.05$ of $91.7$, $67.5$ and $50.3$, respectively. A third gives the six exact values $1100/13$, $220/3$, $48500/869$, $9700/241$, $9700/161$ and $48500/677$. A fourth asserts that $L(44/48,3)=11/14>H(291/579,3)=291/387$ and $L(44/48,4)=11/15<H(291/579,4)=97/121$, so that the shooting gallery and needle exchange intervals are disjoint at $\gamma=3$ and overlap at $\gamma=4$ also with the proportions from the counts. The counts are inferred from the sample sizes and percentages of Section 4. The closed form is taken as given here, and its derivation from (2) and (3) is the subject of a separate Lean statement.
text.headline: Table 1, six entries, as corrected
text.location: Table 1, p. 238 (PDF p. 4)

text.body: Two Lean statements cover the first two sentences of the paragraph, which say that the bounds depend on $\alpha$ and $\beta$ only through $\gamma$ and that $\gamma=1$ is selection with equal probabilities. Let $n\geqslant 1$ and let $y_1,\ldots,y_n$ be real. The first statement asserts that, if $0<\alpha\leqslant\beta\leqslant 1$ and $0<\alpha'\leqslant\beta'\leqslant 1$ satisfy $\beta/\alpha=\beta'/\alpha'$, then the set of values of $w'y/(w'1_n)$ over $[1/\beta,1/\alpha]^n$ equals the set of values over $[1/\beta',1/\alpha']^n$. It asserts further that, if $\beta/\alpha=1$, this set is the single point $\sum_iy_i/n$. The second statement asserts that, for $\gamma=1$, the box is the single point $(1/\alpha,\ldots,1/\alpha)$ and both bounds equal the sample mean. The bounds are represented as the infimum and the supremum of the set of values. Note that the equality of the two sets is stronger than the equality of the bounds, and that the outcomes need not be in increasing order. The last sentence of the paragraph, on the meaning of $\gamma=5$, is an interpretation and has no Lean statement.
text.headline: Section 3.1, the paragraph after equation (5)
text.location: Section 3.1, the first two sentences of the paragraph after equation (5), p. 236 (PDF p. 2)

text.body: The Lean statement asserts Lemma 1 for the vector $w^{\mathrm H}$ of Proposition 1 and for the vector $w^{\mathrm L}$ with the cut point as corrected in P025-E001. Let $n\geqslant 1$, $y_1\leqslant\cdots\leqslant y_n$ and $\gamma\geqslant 1$, and let $k^{\mathrm L}$ and $k^{\mathrm H}$ be the smallest $k\in\{0,\ldots,n-1\}$ that satisfy the corrected lower rule and the upper rule, respectively. The statement asserts that $y_i=y_j$ implies $w^{\mathrm L}_i=w^{\mathrm L}_j$ and $w^{\mathrm H}_i=w^{\mathrm H}_j$, for all $i$ and $j$. The printed lemma concerns adjacent indices $k$ and $k+1$. For outcomes in increasing order the two forms are equivalent. The weights are multiplied by $\beta$, so that their values are $1$ and $\gamma$, which does not change which weights are equal. The cases in which all outcomes are equal or $\gamma=1$ are included. With the printed rule for $k^{\mathrm L}$ the cut point is always $0$ and all entries of $w^{\mathrm L}$ are equal, and the statement uses the corrected rule for this reason.
text.headline: Lemma 1
text.location: p. 237 (PDF p. 3); supplementary material, p. 1

text.body: The Lean statement asserts the display. Let $n\geqslant 1$, $y_i\in\{0,1\}$ for all $i$, $p=\sum_iy_i/n$, $0<\alpha\leqslant\beta\leqslant 1$ and $\gamma=\beta/\alpha$. The statement asserts that the set of values of $w'y/(w'1_n)$, as $w$ ranges over $[1/\beta,1/\alpha]^n$, is the interval $\left[\frac{p}{\gamma(1-p)+p},\ \frac{\gamma p}{(1-p)+\gamma p}\right].$ The cases $p=0$, $p=1$ and $\gamma=1$, in which both endpoints equal $p$, are included, and the outcomes need not be in increasing order. The left side of the printed display is the set of values of $\hat\mu$ as the $\pi_i$ range over $[\alpha,\beta]$, and it is represented by the weights $w_i=1/\pi_i$ of the sampled units. The printed display has $\pi_N$, although the estimator depends on $\pi_1,\ldots,\pi_n$ only. The statement concerns the set of values directly and does not mention Lemma 1 or the cut points of Proposition 1.
text.headline: Section 3.1, the closed form of the bounds for a dichotomous outcome
text.location: Unnumbered display after Lemma 1, p. 237 (PDF p. 3)

text.body: The Lean statement asserts Proposition 3 with Assumptions 1 and 2 as hypotheses. It reads the printed $\mu_h^{\mathrm H}$ and $\mu_h^{\mathrm L}$ as the estimators $\hat\mu_h^{\mathrm H}$ and $\hat\mu_h^{\mathrm L}$ of Assumption 1, and it requires Assumption 2 for the integers $0\leqslant k<|Y|$, at which $y_{(k+1)}$ is defined (see P025-E005). As in the statement for the proposition as corrected, the design is a probability distribution on finitely many draws with $0<\alpha\leqslant\pi_i\leqslant\beta\leqslant 1$, and the replications are its infinite product. The estimators and the limits $\mu_-$ and $\mu_+$ are the infimum and the supremum of the ratio over the box of weights, for the pooled sample and for the totals $\Pi_j$, respectively. The statement asserts that, for almost every sequence of draws, the pooled sample is nonempty for all large $h$, and $\hat\mu_h^{\mathrm L}\to\mu_-$ and $\hat\mu_h^{\mathrm H}\to\mu_+$. It differs from the statement for the corrected proposition only in the added hypothesis of Assumption 2. A second statement gives the step of the supplementary proof in which Assumption 2 is used. For the same ordered outcomes and probability bounds, let $p_j>0$ and $0\leqslant k^*<|Y|$, and let $G^+_k(p)$ be the left side of the rule for $k_+$ with $p_j$ in place of $\Pi_j$. The statement asserts that, if $G^+_{k^*}(p)<y_{(k^*+1)}$, and $G^+_{k^*-1}(p)>y_{(k^*)}$ when $k^*\geqslant 1$, then the rule returns $k_+=k^*$ and the vector with this cut point attains the maximum of the ratio over the box. The words “almost everywhere” refer to the joint distribution of the replications.
text.headline: Proposition 3, as printed
text.location: p. 238 (PDF p. 4); supplementary material, p. 2
